reason: E1 directly supports the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer from an Hf coating and its effectiveness in preventing oxidation and surface degradation, but it addresses oxidation in air, not molten aluminum corrosion. E2 shows HfB2 has superior oxidation resistance among diborides, but does not involve an Hf-rich surface treatment or molten aluminum exposure. The key premise that HfO2 will limit dissolution in molten aluminum is not directly supported by the cited evidence.
premises: Hf-rich coatings can form a dense, protective HfO2 layer upon high-temperature oxidation
HfO2 layers improve oxidation resistance and prevent surface degradation in extreme environments
HfB2 exhibits superior oxidation resistance among individual diborides in high-entropy boride systems
The protective HfO2 layer acts as a barrier to limit substrate dissolution and contact with the environment
The coating must remain intact and adherent to maintain protection
